To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the peak electron beam density increases by a factor 3 when the Twiss parameters are taken into account, and that the electron density profile in the modulator is not uniform.
the electron beam is compressed by the ions in the modulator, and that the electron beam density in the modulators is increased by a factor of $\sim$3.

the peak density in the CEC modulator can be increased by a factor of ~3, and the modulator length can be shortened by a factor of $\sim$ 1.5, by increasing the Twiss parameters of the electron beam in the modulator.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physics of the modulator and its effect on electron cooling.
the development of the modulator section of the CEC experiment, and the effects of the ion beam on the electron beam.
the development of a 3D PIC code for simulating the dynamics of an electron beam in a modulator.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the simulations presented here are in agreement with previous simulations, and show that the electron density can be increased by a factor of about 3, as compared to the case where the electron beam has an infinite transverse extent.
we are in a good position to understand the modulator physics and are now ready for the next step of including a full 3D model of the modulator and the first cooler section.
the simulations presented here demonstrate that the electron beam can be focused and modulated as designed, and the resulting electron beam is sufficiently dense to cool the ions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the electron beam density is not a constant, but rather varies in time and space.

we have developed and validated an efficient 3D simulation framework to model the electron density perturbation and electron beam dynamics in a coherent electron cooler, and that we have shown the importance of including the transverse electron density profile and focusing in the simulations.
the modulator is a viable component of a coherent electron cooling system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the electron beam density can be increased significantly without compromising the electron cooling process.
the density perturbations in the electron beam can be reduced by a factor of $\sim 2$ when the electron beam has the correct transverse extent.

the electron density can be increased significantly in a modulator without significantly increasing the electron beam emittance, and that the electron beam density in the modulators can be tailored for optimal electron cooling performance.
